title: Trauma primary survey (ABCDE)
subtitle: The first ten minutes

sources.org: American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma
sources.title: Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) Student Course Manual

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Major trauma: assessment and initial management (NG39)

red_flags.text: Noisy breathing, stridor, hoarseness or an expanding neck haematoma. The airway is closing.
Tracheal deviation with distended neck veins and a silent hemithorax.
Systolic pressure that does not respond, or responds only transiently, to the first fluid or blood.
GCS falling by 2 or more, a unilateral dilated pupil, or a new focal deficit.
A pelvis that is unstable on imaging, in a shocked patient. Do not spring the pelvis repeatedly.

do_now.text: Catastrophic external haemorrhage first: direct pressure, then a tourniquet high and tight for a limb, then a haemostatic dressing for a junctional bleed.
Airway with manual in-line cervical spine stabilisation. Talk to the patient: a normal voice is a patent airway and an adequate perfusing pressure at that moment.
High-flow oxygen, two large-bore cannulae, bloods including group and crossmatch, and activate the major haemorrhage protocol if shocked.
Decompress a tension pneumothorax on clinical grounds. Do not wait for a radiograph.

assess.text: A: patency, obstruction, burns to the face or airway, expanding haematoma. Anticipate, do not react.
B: respiratory rate, chest expansion, percussion, air entry, oxygen saturation. Look for the six early killers separately.
C: pulse, capillary refill, blood pressure, external bleeding, and the five places blood hides - chest, abdomen, pelvis, long bones, on the floor.
D: GCS, pupils, lateralising signs, capillary glucose. Record the components of GCS, not just the total.
E: expose fully, then cover. Hypothermia is part of the lethal triad and it is the part you cause.
Score injury severity for audit and transfer discussion, never to decide the next action.

investigate.text: Chest and pelvis radiographs in the resuscitation room for the unstable patient.
FAST or eFAST for free fluid. A negative scan in a shocked patient excludes nothing.
Venous or arterial gas with lactate and base deficit: the best early marker of occult hypoperfusion.
Whole-body CT for the stabilised patient with a significant mechanism. The unstable patient goes to theatre, not to the scanner.

resuscitate.text: Blood, not crystalloid, for haemorrhagic shock. Limit clear fluid; it dilutes clotting factors and raises pressure off a clot.
Tranexamic acid as early as possible in significant traumatic haemorrhage; the benefit falls away with delay.
Keep the patient warm actively: warmed fluids, forced-air blanket, and stop exposing once the survey is done.
Bind an unstable pelvis at the level of the greater trochanters, not the iliac crests.

definitive.text: Stop the bleeding. In a non-responder that means theatre or interventional radiology now, with resuscitation continuing on the way.
Damage control surgery for the physiologically exhausted patient: control haemorrhage and contamination, pack, close temporarily, correct physiology in intensive care, return later.
Only after the primary survey and its interventions are complete does the secondary survey begin. Reassess from A whenever the patient deteriorates.

escalate.text: Call the trauma team leader, anaesthesia and blood bank early rather than accurately.
Transfer to a major trauma centre for penetrating torso injury, an unstable pelvis, a significant head injury needing neurosurgery, or any injury beyond local capability.
Never transfer a patient whose airway or haemorrhage is uncontrolled. Fix A and C, then move.

notes: The order is the message: a problem found at A is treated at A before anyone moves to B.
Reassess after every intervention, and start again at A on any deterioration. Most missed injuries are missed because nobody went back to the beginning.
The review date on the ATLS reference has passed; confirm the current edition before teaching from this page.
